stimulus.title: The Machine That Walked
stimulus.text: The earliest ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. Built in 1817, it was a wooden frame on two wheels that a rider straddled and pushed along with the feet, like walking while seated. People mocked it, and rutted roads made it impractical, so it soon faded. Decades passed before inventors added pedals, then a chain, then air-filled tires that smoothed the ride. Each change drew new riders, and by the 1890s the bicycle had become a craze. It offered something rare for the time: cheap, independent travel that needed no horse and no rails. For many people, especially those long denied easy movement, the machine quietly widened the boundaries of daily life.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the library obtained many of its scrolls by

choices.text: forbidding any visitor from bringing a book through its doors
choices.rationale: Scholars were welcomed, not forbidden.

choices.text: copying texts that happened to arrive aboard ships at the harbor
choices.rationale: Correct. Scrolls aboard docking ships were searched and copied.

choices.text: having its own scribes write out every single scroll purely from memory
choices.rationale: Copying, not memory, is described.

choices.text: buying them only from a small number of local city sellers
choices.rationale: The passage describes copying ships' scrolls, not only local purchases.

questions.explanation: The ship-copying practice explains how the collection grew.

stimulus.title: A House for Every Book
stimulus.text: The ancient library at Alexandria aimed at something audacious: to gather a copy of every book in the world. Ships docking at the harbor were searched, and any scrolls aboard were copied; sometimes the library kept the original and returned the copy. Scholars from distant lands came to read, argue, and write, and the collection may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls. We know less than we would like about how the library declined, and popular stories of a single great fire oversimplify a slow loss across centuries. Still, the idea behind it endured. The dream of one place that holds all knowledge has reappeared, in new forms, ever since.

questions.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the author regards folk weather signs as

choices.text: more accurate than any modern forecasting method
choices.rationale: The passage says forecasting absorbed the best parts, implying it is reliable.

choices.text: a mix of useful observation and unreliable belief
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says folk knowledge mixed keen observation with superstition.

choices.text: entirely useless and worth completely ignoring
choices.rationale: The passage credits some folk signs with real wisdom.

choices.text: purely superstition with no basis in real conditions
choices.rationale: Some signs, like the hazy moon, reflect real conditions.

questions.explanation: The author views folk signs as a blend of insight and superstition.

stimulus.title: Reading the Weather Before Radio
stimulus.text: Long before satellites mapped storms from orbit, farmers learned to read the sky and the land for signs of coming weather. A ring of haze around the moon, the smell of soil before rain, the behavior of swallows flying low: such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down through families. Much of this folk knowledge was unreliable, mixing keen observation with superstition. Yet some of it held real wisdom, since the conditions that produce a hazy moon truly can precede rain. Modern forecasting has not so much replaced this older watching as absorbed its best parts, trading the rooster's crow for the radar's sweep.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that the octopus cannot perceive its own display?

choices.text: the statement that its color can bloom or vanish in less than a second
choices.rationale: Speed of change does not address perception.

choices.text: the statement that each sac of pigment is ringed by a band of muscle
choices.rationale: The muscle ring explains how color appears, not whether the animal sees it.

choices.text: the statement that the octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own
choices.rationale: Lacking bones is unrelated to perceiving color.

choices.text: the statement that the octopus is colorblind and cannot see the hues it makes
choices.rationale: Correct. Colorblindness directly explains why it cannot see the hues it makes.

questions.explanation: The claim about perception is supported specifically by the detail that the animal is colorblind.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Beneath its skin lie millions of tiny sacs of pigment, each ringed by muscle. When the muscles pull, the sacs widen and color blooms; when they relax, the color vanishes. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that maps improved as exploration advanced?

choices.text: the statement that some old maps added sea monsters as a form of decoration
choices.rationale: Decorative monsters do not show improvement.

choices.text: the statement that mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never actually seen
choices.rationale: Imagined mountains describe the early errors, not the improvement.

choices.text: the statement that the guesses were slowly corrected as explorers returned with measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Corrections following explorers' measurements show improvement over time.

choices.text: the statement that a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make
choices.rationale: Hidden difficulty is a reflection, not evidence of improvement.

questions.explanation: Improvement is supported by corrections from returning explorers.

stimulus.title: The Edge of the Map
stimulus.text: Old maps are full of guesses. Where knowledge ran out, mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never seen and coastlines that bent the wrong way. Some added sea monsters, less from belief than from a need to decorate the unknown. As explorers returned with measurements, the guesses were slowly corrected, and the monsters swam off the page. But a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make. Every clean line was once a question, settled only by someone willing to sail past the edge of what was known and come back with an answer.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that writing helped Tomas understand his own feelings?

choices.text: the detail that the first version listed the small triumphs of his new city
choices.rationale: The cheerful list hid, rather than revealed, his feelings.

choices.text: the detail that he wrote the letter three times before stopping
choices.rationale: Writing it three times shows effort, not the self-understanding itself.

choices.text: the detail that writing the words let him admit how far from home he felt
choices.rationale: Correct. This directly states that the writing let him admit his feelings.

choices.text: the detail that he kept the third version folded in a drawer
choices.rationale: Keeping the letter in a drawer does not by itself show understanding.

questions.explanation: Self-understanding is shown by the line about admitting how far from home he felt.

stimulus.title: The Unsent Letter
stimulus.text: Tomas wrote the letter three times before he stopped trying to send it. In the first version he was cheerful, listing the small triumphs of his new city as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown. In the second he was honest, and the page filled with everything he missed until it embarrassed him. The third version said almost nothing at all. He kept that one folded in a drawer. Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that the cold preserves the seeds' ability to grow?

choices.text: the statement that the vault serves as a backup against crop loss
choices.rationale: Calling it a backup states purpose, not preservation.

choices.text: the statement that even after decades the stored seeds can still sprout
choices.rationale: Correct. Sprouting after decades shows preservation of viability.

choices.text: the statement that the vault is built deep inside a frozen mountain
choices.rationale: The location alone does not show preserved viability.

choices.text: the statement that the seed varieties were gathered from all around the world
choices.rationale: The seeds' origins do not address viability.

questions.explanation: Preserved viability is shown by sprouting after decades.

stimulus.title: A Vault for Seeds
stimulus.text: Deep inside a frozen mountain, a vault holds something more valuable than gold: seeds. Hundreds of thousands of varieties of crops, gathered from around the world, rest in sealed packets at temperatures far below freezing. The cold slows the seeds' aging to a crawl, so that even after decades they can still sprout. The vault is a backup. If a war, flood, or disease wipes out a crop somewhere, a sample can be withdrawn and grown again. Its keepers hope it will rarely be needed, the way one hopes never to use a fire extinguisher. Its value lies precisely in being ready and almost never used.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that automation improved reliability?

choices.text: the statement that the keepers were gradually withdrawn over time
choices.rationale: Withdrawal of keepers is the human cost, not the reliability claim.

choices.text: the statement that the lights still shine, more reliably than ever before
choices.rationale: Correct. 'More reliably than ever' directly supports improved reliability.

choices.text: the statement that isolation made the work of the keeper lonely
choices.rationale: Loneliness describes the old role, not reliability.

choices.text: the statement that storms made the keeper's nightly work on the tower dangerous
choices.rationale: Dangerous storms concern the old hardship, not reliability gains.

questions.explanation: Improved reliability is stated directly in that detail.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Storms made the work dangerous, and isolation made it lonely, but ships depended on that faithful beam. In the twentieth century, automation arrived. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that Nadia's playing improved on the loaner?

choices.text: the detail that she returned the borrowed violin to its case afterward
choices.rationale: Returning the violin does not show improved playing.

choices.text: the detail that two of her school violin's pegs slipped every lesson
choices.rationale: Slipping pegs describe the old instrument, not improvement.

choices.text: the detail that she had nearly refused the instrument to begin with
choices.rationale: Her near-refusal is about hesitation, not improvement.

choices.text: the detail that notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily
choices.rationale: Correct. The ease of once-difficult notes shows improved playing.

questions.explanation: Improvement is shown by once-hard notes arriving easily.

stimulus.title: The Borrowed Violin
stimulus.text: Nadia had practiced on a school instrument so battered that two of its pegs slipped during every lesson. When her teacher handed her a loaner violin for the recital, she nearly refused; it felt wrong to play something so fine. But as she drew the bow across the strings, the tone opened like a window onto a bright street. Notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily, as if the instrument had been waiting for her. Afterward, returning it to its case, she understood that her old struggles had not been wasted. The fine violin had simply revealed the player she had quietly become.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that current systems limit glass recycling?

choices.text: the statement that much glass ends up in landfills because collection is uneven
choices.rationale: Correct. Uneven collection sending glass to landfills shows a system limitation.

choices.text: the statement that glass can be melted down and remade again and again without losing quality
choices.rationale: Quality retention is a property of glass, not a system failure.

choices.text: the statement that a bottle recycled today can become a bottle next month
choices.rationale: This describes the ideal, not the limit.

choices.text: the statement that the material is willing while our systems need redesigning
choices.rationale: 'The material is willing' is figurative, not specific evidence.

questions.explanation: System limits are supported by the uneven-collection detail.

stimulus.title: The Endless Material
stimulus.text: Glass has a quiet superpower: it can be melted down and remade again and again without losing quality. A bottle recycled today can become a bottle next month, then another after that, in a loop that, in principle, never wears out. Compared with this ideal, reality lags. Much glass still ends up in landfills because collection is uneven and because mixing colors lowers the value of the recycled material. Sorting by color and keeping glass out of general trash would let more of it re-enter the loop. The material is willing; it is our systems, the author suggests, that need redesigning.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that marshes can keep pace with rising seas?

choices.text: the statement that for many years marshes were drained and filled without much thought
choices.rationale: Past draining concerns history, not keeping pace.

choices.text: the statement that roots beneath the mud store carbon
choices.rationale: Carbon storage is a separate benefit, not pace with the sea.

choices.text: the statement that the grasses trap sediment, letting the marsh build itself upward
choices.rationale: Correct. Trapping sediment to build upward directly shows the marsh keeping pace with the sea.

choices.text: the statement that the marsh can look like flat, muddy wasteland
choices.rationale: The marsh's plain appearance does not address rising seas.

questions.explanation: Keeping pace with the sea is supported by the sediment-trapping detail.

stimulus.title: The Quiet Buffer
stimulus.text: Where the land meets the sea, a salt marsh can look like wasteland: flat, muddy, and crossed by winding channels. Yet this drab landscape does remarkable work. Its dense grasses slow incoming waves, blunting the force of storms before they reach homes inland. The same grasses trap sediment, letting the marsh build itself upward as the sea slowly rises. Beneath the mud, roots store carbon that might otherwise warm the air. For years, marshes were drained and filled without much thought. Only later did people recognize that the unglamorous marsh had been protecting them all along, asking nothing in return.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that bats can sense whether an object is moving?

choices.text: the statement that bats call at pitches too high for humans to hear
choices.rationale: The pitch of the call does not address motion sensing.

choices.text: the statement that subtle shifts in the returning sound reveal motion toward or away
choices.rationale: Correct. Shifts in the returning sound directly indicate motion.

choices.text: the statement that the world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes
choices.rationale: The 'built of sound' image is general, not motion-specific.

choices.text: the statement that the bat judges distance from the delay of the echo
choices.rationale: Echo delay reveals distance, not motion direction.

questions.explanation: Motion sensing is supported by the 'subtle shifts' detail.

stimulus.title: Seeing With Sound
stimulus.text: A bat hunting in pitch darkness does not bump into things. It calls out, often at pitches too high for humans to hear, and listens for the echoes that bounce back. From the delay between call and echo, the bat judges how far away an object is; from subtle shifts in the returning sound, it can tell whether the object is moving toward it or away. A moth's fluttering wing returns a different echo than a still leaf. So precise is this sense that some bats can snatch an insect from the air in total darkness. The world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that the dance conveys distance?

choices.text: the statement that the dance passes its information without any sound
choices.rationale: Absence of sound concerns the medium, not distance.

choices.text: the statement that other bees crowd around the dancer and follow its movements closely
choices.rationale: Followers show interest, not the distance code.

choices.text: the statement that the length of the bee's straight run signals distance
choices.rationale: Correct. Run length signaling distance directly supports the distance claim.

choices.text: the statement that the bee dances on a vertical comb in total darkness
choices.rationale: The setting does not address distance.

questions.explanation: Distance is supported by the 'length of the run' detail.

stimulus.title: Dances in the Dark
stimulus.text: A foraging honeybee that finds a rich patch of flowers cannot simply tell the hive where to go. Instead, it dances. On the vertical comb, in darkness, the bee runs a straight line while waggling its body, then loops back to repeat the move. The angle of that straight run, measured against the pull of gravity, encodes the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the run signals distance. Watching bees crowd around and follow, researchers realized they were seeing a kind of symbolic language, one that passes precise information without sight, sound, or a single spoken word.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that fog harvesting can meaningfully add to a water supply?

choices.text: the statement that the mesh nets require regular upkeep to keep working
choices.rationale: Upkeep is a limitation, not a benefit.

choices.text: the statement that moist air rolls in toward the hillsides from the sea
choices.rationale: Incoming moist air explains the source, not the amount collected.

choices.text: the statement that a single large net can collect many liters on a good day
choices.rationale: Correct. The volume collected shows a meaningful contribution.

choices.text: the statement that the method works only where fog is frequent and winds are steady
choices.rationale: Frequency is a condition, not the yield.

questions.explanation: The 'many liters' figure supports the usefulness claim.

stimulus.title: Catching Water From Air
stimulus.text: In a few dry coastal regions, drinking water can be harvested from fog. Tall mesh nets are strung across hillsides where moist air rolls in from the sea. As the fog drifts through, droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and trickle down into troughs and storage tanks. A single large net can collect many liters on a good day, enough to supplement a village's supply. The method is not a cure-all: it works only where fog is frequent and winds are steady, and the nets need upkeep. Yet in the right place, it turns a passing cloud into a dependable resource, using little more than gravity and patience.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that a kelp forest can collapse quickly?

choices.text: the statement that kelp forests shelter fish, snails, and otters
choices.rationale: Sheltering animals describes richness, not collapse.

choices.text: the statement that giant kelp can stretch dozens of meters toward the surface
choices.rationale: The kelp's height describes its size, not a collapse.

choices.text: the statement that the kelp can grow half a meter in a single day
choices.rationale: Fast growth describes vigor, not collapse.

choices.text: the statement that without otters, urchins multiply and graze the kelp to bare rock
choices.rationale: Correct. Urchins grazing the kelp to bare rock directly shows a collapse.

questions.explanation: Collapse is supported by the urchins-graze-to-bare-rock detail.

stimulus.title: Forests Beneath the Waves
stimulus.text: Off some cool, rocky coasts grow forests that no hiker will ever walk through. Giant kelp, anchored to the seafloor, can stretch dozens of meters toward the surface, swaying in the current like trees in wind. These kelp forests shelter fish, snails, and otters, much as a woodland shelters birds and deer. The kelp grows astonishingly fast, sometimes half a meter in a single day, drinking sunlight near the surface. But the forest is fragile. Where otters vanish, sea urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to bare rock, leaving a barren the divers call an urchin desert. A single missing animal can unmake a whole forest.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that coral bands reveal past water temperature?

choices.text: the statement that a coral skeleton grows in fine bands like tree rings
choices.rationale: The tree-ring comparison concerns growth, not temperature.

choices.text: the statement that the chemistry trapped in each band hints at the water's temperature
choices.rationale: Correct. The trapped chemistry directly links the bands to past temperature.

choices.text: the statement that the record can stretch back several centuries
choices.rationale: The record's length does not address temperature.

choices.text: the statement that reading the bands is like reading a language no one designed to be read
choices.rationale: The reading-difficulty image does not establish temperature.

questions.explanation: Temperature is supported specifically by the trapped-chemistry detail.

stimulus.title: The Coral That Keeps Time
stimulus.text: A coral skeleton grows in fine bands, much like the rings of a tree. In bright, warm months the coral lays down thick layers; in cooler, dimmer months the layers thin. By slicing a coral and counting these bands, researchers can read a record of past seasons stretching back centuries. Even better, the chemistry trapped in each band hints at the water's temperature when it formed. So a single old coral can serve as a kind of diary, written not in words but in stone, recording conditions long before anyone thought to measure them. The challenge is learning to read a language no one designed to be read.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that some seeds rely on animals eating them?

choices.text: the statement that some seeds grow papery wings and spin away on the wind like tiny helicopters
choices.rationale: Winged seeds rely on wind, not on being eaten.

choices.text: the statement that a plant cannot walk to find open ground
choices.rationale: The opening notes a plant cannot walk, unrelated to being eaten.

choices.text: the statement that some seeds hide in sweet fruit so an animal eats and carries them off
choices.rationale: Correct. Hiding in fruit to be eaten and carried directly supports the claim.

choices.text: the statement that some seeds wear hooks that snag passing fur
choices.rationale: Hooked seeds rely on fur, not on being eaten.

questions.explanation: Reliance on being eaten is supported by the sweet-fruit detail.

stimulus.title: Travelers Without Legs
stimulus.text: A plant cannot walk, yet its seeds must somehow leave the shadow of the parent and find open ground. Evolution has answered this need with a surprising range of tricks. Some seeds grow papery wings and spin away on the wind like tiny helicopters. Others wear hooks that snag the fur of passing animals, hitching a ride for miles. Still others hide inside sweet fruit, counting on an animal to eat them and carry them off, depositing them far away. Each method is a kind of bargain struck with the world around the plant. The seed that travels farthest is often the one with the best chance to grow where the parent's shade cannot reach.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that public voting could intimidate voters?

choices.text: the statement that a worker might think twice before voting against a watching boss
choices.rationale: Correct. The hesitant worker example directly shows intimidation under public voting.

choices.text: the statement that the change shifted power toward the ordinary voter
choices.rationale: The power shift is the effect of reform, not the intimidation itself.

choices.text: the statement that reformers pushed for a printed ballot dropped in a box
choices.rationale: The reformers' push is the response, not evidence of intimidation.

choices.text: the statement that it is easy to assume voting has always been private
choices.rationale: The opening assumption does not show intimidation.

questions.explanation: Intimidation is supported by the watching-boss example.

stimulus.title: The Secret Ballot
stimulus.text: It is easy to assume voting has always been private, but for a long time it was not. In many places people voted aloud or by a show of hands, in full view of employers, landlords, and neighbors. That openness invited pressure: a worker might think twice before voting against a boss who could see the choice. Reformers pushed for a printed ballot, marked alone and dropped in a box, so that no one need fear retaliation for an honest vote. The change seemed minor, a mere matter of paper, yet it shifted real power toward the ordinary voter, who could now decide without an audience.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that locks rely on simple means?

choices.text: the statement that distant towns became trading partners
choices.rationale: Trading partnerships are an effect, not evidence of simplicity.

choices.text: the statement that the lock relies on nothing more exotic than gravity and patience
choices.rationale: Correct. 'Nothing more exotic than gravity and patience' directly shows simple means.

choices.text: the statement that a boat enters a chamber with gates at each end and the gates close behind it
choices.rationale: The chamber description explains how a lock works, not its simplicity.

choices.text: the statement that shallow rivers became highways of commerce
choices.rationale: Rivers becoming highways is an effect, not evidence of simplicity.

questions.explanation: Simplicity is supported by the 'gravity and patience' detail.

stimulus.title: Stairs for Boats
stimulus.text: Rivers do not run level, and for centuries that simple fact blocked boats from traveling far inland. The lock changed things. A lock is a chamber with gates at each end; a boat enters, the gates close, and water is let in or drained out until the boat rises or falls to the next stretch of river. String several locks together, and a vessel can climb a hillside the way a person climbs a staircase. The engineering is humble, relying on nothing more exotic than gravity and patience, yet it knit distant towns into trading partners and turned shallow rivers into highways of commerce.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that Mr. Owusu paid close attention to individual customers?

choices.text: the detail that he recalled which customer's child disliked onions
choices.rationale: Correct. Remembering a specific child's dislike shows close attention to individuals.

choices.text: the detail that the market felt larger after he retired
choices.rationale: The market feeling larger is the effect of his absence, not his attention.

choices.text: the detail that he set out the same vegetables every Saturday
choices.rationale: Setting out the same vegetables shows routine, not personal attention.

choices.text: the detail that his stall was, for years, just one among many
choices.rationale: Being one stall among many does not show attentiveness.

questions.explanation: Close personal attention is shown by his recalling the child's dislike of onions.

stimulus.title: The Stall That Listened
stimulus.text: Every Saturday, Mr. Owusu set out the same vegetables on the same table, and for years his stall was just one among many. What set him apart, his daughter noticed, was not his prices but his memory. He recalled which customer's child disliked onions, who was cooking for a crowd that weekend, who had been ill and needed something gentle. He would set aside a perfect tomato for one regular and toss an extra handful of beans to another. People did not return only for the produce; they returned because, at his stall, they were known. When he finally retired, the market felt larger and lonelier, though not a single other stall had closed.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that spices were once extremely valuable?

choices.text: the statement that a handful of pepper could rival a handful of silver
choices.rationale: Correct. Pepper rivaling silver directly shows its great value.

choices.text: the statement that spices grew only in distant lands
choices.rationale: Distant origins explain scarcity, not value directly.

choices.text: the statement that merchants guarded their trade routes jealously
choices.rationale: Guarding routes shows protectiveness, not the value figure.

choices.text: the statement that sea voyages redrew the map of the world
choices.rationale: Redrawing the map is an effect, not evidence of value.

questions.explanation: The pepper-rivaling-silver detail supports the value claim.

stimulus.title: The Price of Pepper
stimulus.text: There was a time when a handful of black pepper could rival a handful of silver. The spice grew only in distant lands, and by the time it reached a European market it had passed through many hands, each adding a markup. Merchants guarded their routes jealously and spread tall tales about how spices were harvested, partly to discourage rivals. The high prices drove sailors to seek their own sea paths to the source, voyages that redrew the map of the world. In the end, the very abundance those voyages produced made spices ordinary, and the fortunes built on rarity quietly dissolved.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that lichens help create soil?

choices.text: the statement that the alga makes food from sunlight while sheltered inside
choices.rationale: The alga's feeding explains survival, not soil formation.

choices.text: the statement that a lichen is a partnership of fungus and alga living as one
choices.rationale: The partnership detail explains what a lichen is, not soil-making.

choices.text: the statement that acids from the lichen crack the rock and its dead tissue mixes with grit
choices.rationale: Correct. Cracking rock and leaving tissue that mixes into grit directly forms soil.

choices.text: the statement that the lichen is later crowded out by the very community it made possible
choices.rationale: Being crowded out is the outcome, not the soil-making process.

questions.explanation: Soil formation is supported by the acid-and-tissue detail.

stimulus.title: First on the Rock
stimulus.text: When a bare rock is left exposed, the first life to arrive is often a lichen, a strange partnership of fungus and alga living as one. The fungus grips the stone and gathers moisture; the alga, sheltered inside, makes food from sunlight. Together they need no soil at all. As a lichen grows, it slowly releases acids that crack the rock surface, and its dead tissue mixes with grit to form the first thin crumbs of soil. Years later, mosses and small plants can take root in that beginning. The lichen will likely be crowded out by the very community it made possible, an unsung founder of the green world that follows.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that printing dramatically increased the number of books?

choices.text: the statement that copying a single book by hand could occupy a scribe for a year
choices.rationale: This describes the old method, not the increase.

choices.text: the statement that many scholars still prized their handwritten volumes
choices.rationale: This shows continued demand for manuscripts, not the scale of printing.

choices.text: the statement that within fifty years presses had produced millions of books
choices.rationale: Correct. The figure of millions in fifty years directly shows the surge in output.

choices.text: the statement that Gutenberg cast each individual letter out of metal
choices.rationale: This explains the method but not the resulting quantity.

questions.explanation: The claim about volume is supported by the 'millions of books' figure.

stimulus.title: Letters of Lead
stimulus.text: Before the 1450s, a book in Europe was copied by hand, a task that could occupy a scribe for a year. Johannes Gutenberg changed that arithmetic. By casting individual letters in metal, he could arrange them into a page, print hundreds of copies, then rearrange the same letters for the next page. The cost of a book did not fall overnight, and many scholars still prized handwritten volumes. But within fifty years, presses across the continent had produced millions of books. Ideas that once crept from city to city now traveled in bulk, and a reader in one town could hold the exact words read by a stranger far away.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that volcanic regions attract dense settlement?

choices.text: the statement that the same mountain that feeds the fields can also threaten them
choices.rationale: The threat detail concerns risk, not attraction.

choices.text: the statement that slopes near certain volcanoes are crowded with farms and villages

Crops planted in it can grow unusually well, which is why slopes near certain volcanoes are crowded with farms and villages. The bargain is uneasy: the same mountain that feeds the fields can also threaten them. Farmers weigh the steady gift of rich soil against the rare but real danger overhead, and generation after generation, many choose to stay.

In this state it can endure boiling heat, the vacuum of space, and doses of radiation that would kill nearly any other animal. Years later, a single drop of water can revive it. Scientists are still untangling how the tardigrade protects its cells, but one clue is a special set of proteins that seem to harden into glass, cradling delicate structures until water returns.

stimulus.text: A white-crowned sparrow raised near San Francisco does not sing quite like one raised a hundred miles north. Young sparrows learn these dialects by listening to adult males during a brief window in their first months. A bird that hears no song in that window grows up to sing a thin, simplified tune. The dialects can drift over generations, much as human accents do, so a recording made decades ago may sound subtly foreign to the birds singing in the same meadow today.

stimulus.title: The Number That Was Nothing
stimulus.text: For much of history, there was no symbol for nothing. People counted sheep and coins easily enough, but the idea of writing down an empty amount seemed pointless, even unsettling. The breakthrough came when mathematicians treated zero not as the absence of a number but as a number in its own right, one that could be added, subtracted, and used to hold a place in larger figures. With zero, the difference between 5 and 50 could be written clearly, and long calculations grew far simpler. A concept that once felt like a riddle became the quiet hinge on which much of modern mathematics turns.

stimulus.title: Small Pieces, Wide Reach
stimulus.text: Plastic does not simply vanish. Exposed to sunlight and waves, a bottle or bag breaks into ever-smaller fragments until the pieces are too tiny to see. Researchers caution that the full effects on health are not yet clear, and they warn against easy conclusions. What is clear is that the cheapest fix is also the simplest: keeping plastic out of the environment in the first place, before it can shatter into pieces no net can catch.

stimulus.title: Land Made of Mud
stimulus.text: A great river carries more than water; it carries soil, scoured from distant hills and ground into fine particles. Where the river finally slows and meets the sea, it can no longer hold this load, and the sediment settles out, building flat new land called a delta. Over centuries a delta can grow seaward, fanning into a maze of channels and islands. But the process depends on a steady supply of mud. When dams upstream trap that sediment, the delta is starved; waves carry off more land than the river replaces, and the coastline begins to retreat. What looks like permanent ground is, in truth, a balance constantly being rebuilt.

stimulus.title: When Noon Moved
stimulus.text: Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun overhead at noon. A traveler crossing the country adjusted a watch town by town, and no one minded a few minutes' difference. Railroads made the patchwork intolerable. Trains ran on schedules, and a schedule means nothing if each station defines noon differently; a missed connection could be a matter of life and death. So the railways carved the land into broad zones, each agreeing to share a single time. People grumbled at first about clocks that no longer matched the sun, but the convenience won out. The hour on the wall had become a public agreement rather than a private reading of the sky.

stimulus.title: The Machine That Walked
stimulus.text: The earliest ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. People mocked it, and rutted roads made it impractical, so it soon faded. Decades passed before inventors added pedals, then a chain, then air-filled tires that smoothed the ride. Each change drew new riders, and by the 1890s the bicycle had become a craze. It offered something rare for the time: cheap, independent travel that needed no horse and no rails. For many people, especially those long denied easy movement, the machine quietly widened the boundaries of daily life.

stimulus.title: A House for Every Book
stimulus.text: The ancient library at Alexandria aimed at something audacious: to gather a copy of every book in the world. Scholars from distant lands came to read, argue, and write, and the collection may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls. We know less than we would like about how the library declined, and popular stories of a single great fire oversimplify a slow loss across centuries. Still, the idea behind it endured. The dream of one place that holds all knowledge has reappeared, in new forms, ever since.

stimulus.title: Reading the Weather Before Radio
stimulus.text: Long before satellites mapped storms from orbit, farmers learned to read the sky and the land for signs of coming weather. A ring of haze around the moon, the smell of soil before rain, the behavior of swallows flying low: such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down through families. Much of this folk knowledge was unreliable, mixing keen observation with superstition. Yet some of it held real wisdom, since the conditions that produce a hazy moon truly can precede rain. Modern forecasting has not so much replaced this older watching as absorbed its best parts, trading the rooster's crow for the radar's sweep.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

Beneath the mud, roots store carbon that might otherwise warm the air. For years, marshes were drained and filled without much thought. Only later did people recognize that the unglamorous marsh had been protecting them all along, asking nothing in return.

A moth's fluttering wing returns a different echo than a still leaf. So precise is this sense that some bats can snatch an insect from the air in total darkness. The world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes.

stimulus.title: Dances in the Dark

Watching bees crowd around and follow, researchers realized they were seeing a kind of symbolic language, one that passes precise information without sight, sound, or a single spoken word.

So a single old coral can serve as a kind of diary, written not in words but in stone, recording conditions long before anyone thought to measure them. The challenge is learning to read a language no one designed to be read.

stimulus.title: First on the Rock
stimulus.text: When a bare rock is left exposed, the first life to arrive is often a lichen, a strange partnership of fungus and alga living as one. The fungus grips the stone and gathers moisture; the alga, sheltered inside, makes food from sunlight. Together they need no soil at all. As a lichen grows, it slowly releases acids that crack the rock surface, and its dead tissue mixes with grit to form the first thin crumbs of soil. Years later, mosses and small plants can take root in that beginning. The lichen will likely be crowded out by the very community it made possible, an unsung founder of the green world that follows.

stimulus.title: Letters of Lead
stimulus.text: Before the 1450s, a book in Europe was copied by hand, a task that could occupy a scribe for a year. Johannes Gutenberg changed that arithmetic. By casting individual letters in metal, he could arrange them into a page, print hundreds of copies, then rearrange the same letters for the next page. The cost of a book did not fall overnight, and many scholars still prized handwritten volumes. But within fifty years, presses across the continent had produced millions of books. Ideas that once crept from city to city now traveled in bulk, and a reader in one town could hold the exact words read by a stranger far away.

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, the word “scatters” most nearly means

Correct. The eruption spreads ash widely.

questions.explanation: To 'scatter ash' is to spread it over a wide area.

stimulus.title: Gifts of the Volcano
stimulus.text: It seems strange that people would farm in the shadow of a volcano, but many do, and for good reason. When a volcano erupts, it scatters ash rich in minerals such as potassium and phosphorus. Over years, this ash breaks down into some of the most fertile soil on Earth. Crops planted in it can grow unusually well, which is why slopes near certain volcanoes are crowded with farms and villages. The bargain is uneasy: the same mountain that feeds the fields can also threaten them. Farmers weigh the steady gift of rich soil against the rare but real danger overhead, and generation after generation, many choose to stay.

stimulus.title: The Survivor
stimulus.text: Smaller than a grain of salt, the tardigrade looks almost comical, plodding on eight stubby legs. Its talent, however, is anything but ordinary. When its surroundings dry out, the creature expels most of its water and curls into a husk called a tun. In this state it can endure boiling heat, the vacuum of space, and doses of radiation that would kill nearly any other animal. Years later, a single drop of water can revive it. Scientists are still untangling how the tardigrade protects its cells, but one clue is a special set of proteins that seem to harden into glass, cradling delicate structures until water returns.

stimulus.title: Songs With Accents
stimulus.text: A white-crowned sparrow raised near San Francisco does not sing quite like one raised a hundred miles north. The basic melody is the same, but small flourishes differ from place to place, forming what biologists call song dialects. Young sparrows learn these dialects by listening to adult males during a brief window in their first months. A bird that hears no song in that window grows up to sing a thin, simplified tune. The dialects can drift over generations, much as human accents do, so a recording made decades ago may sound subtly foreign to the birds singing in the same meadow today.

stimulus.title: The Number That Was Nothing
stimulus.text: For much of history, there was no symbol for nothing. People counted sheep and coins easily enough, but the idea of writing down an empty amount seemed pointless, even unsettling. The breakthrough came when mathematicians treated zero not as the absence of a number but as a number in its own right, one that could be added, subtracted, and used to hold a place in larger figures. With zero, the difference between 5 and 50 could be written clearly, and long calculations grew far simpler. A concept that once felt like a riddle became the quiet hinge on which much of modern mathematics turns.

stimulus.title: Small Pieces, Wide Reach
stimulus.text: Plastic does not simply vanish. Exposed to sunlight and waves, a bottle or bag breaks into ever-smaller fragments until the pieces are too tiny to see. These microplastics have turned up in river water, in Arctic ice, and even in the bodies of fish and birds. Because the particles are so small, filtering them out of the ocean is nearly impossible. Researchers caution that the full effects on health are not yet clear, and they warn against easy conclusions. What is clear is that the cheapest fix is also the simplest: keeping plastic out of the environment in the first place, before it can shatter into pieces no net can catch.

questions.explanation: A delta that is 'starved' is deprived of its needed sediment supply.

stimulus.title: Land Made of Mud
stimulus.text: A great river carries more than water; it carries soil, scoured from distant hills and ground into fine particles. Where the river finally slows and meets the sea, it can no longer hold this load, and the sediment settles out, building flat new land called a delta. Over centuries a delta can grow seaward, fanning into a maze of channels and islands. But the process depends on a steady supply of mud. When dams upstream trap that sediment, the delta is starved; waves carry off more land than the river replaces, and the coastline begins to retreat. What looks like permanent ground is, in truth, a balance constantly being rebuilt.

stimulus.title: When Noon Moved
stimulus.text: Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun overhead at noon. A traveler crossing the country adjusted a watch town by town, and no one minded a few minutes' difference. Railroads made the patchwork intolerable. Trains ran on schedules, and a schedule means nothing if each station defines noon differently; a missed connection could be a matter of life and death. So the railways carved the land into broad zones, each agreeing to share a single time. People grumbled at first about clocks that no longer matched the sun, but the convenience won out. The hour on the wall had become a public agreement rather than a private reading of the sky.

Correct. The bicycle expanded the boundaries of daily life.

stimulus.title: The Machine That Walked
stimulus.text: The earliest ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. Built in 1817, it was a wooden frame on two wheels that a rider straddled and pushed along with the feet, like walking while seated. People mocked it, and rutted roads made it impractical, so it soon faded. Decades passed before inventors added pedals, then a chain, then air-filled tires that smoothed the ride. Each change drew new riders, and by the 1890s the bicycle had become a craze. It offered something rare for the time: cheap, independent travel that needed no horse and no rails. For many people, especially those long denied easy movement, the machine quietly widened the boundaries of daily life.

stimulus.title: A House for Every Book
stimulus.text: The ancient library at Alexandria aimed at something audacious: to gather a copy of every book in the world. Ships docking at the harbor were searched, and any scrolls aboard were copied; sometimes the library kept the original and returned the copy. Scholars from distant lands came to read, argue, and write, and the collection may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls. We know less than we would like about how the library declined, and popular stories of a single great fire oversimplify a slow loss across centuries. Still, the idea behind it endured. The dream of one place that holds all knowledge has reappeared, in new forms, ever since.

Correct. Modern forecasting took in and incorporated the best of the old signs.
No literal liquid is soaked up.

questions.explanation: Forecasting 'absorbed' the best parts by taking them in and incorporating them.

stimulus.title: Reading the Weather Before Radio
stimulus.text: Long before satellites mapped storms from orbit, farmers learned to read the sky and the land for signs of coming weather. A ring of haze around the moon, the smell of soil before rain, the behavior of swallows flying low: such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down through families. Much of this folk knowledge was unreliable, mixing keen observation with superstition. Yet some of it held real wisdom, since the conditions that produce a hazy moon truly can precede rain. Modern forecasting has not so much replaced this older watching as absorbed its best parts, trading the rooster's crow for the radar's sweep.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Beneath its skin lie millions of tiny sacs of pigment, each ringed by muscle. When the muscles pull, the sacs widen and color blooms; when they relax, the color vanishes. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

stimulus.title: The Edge of the Map
stimulus.text: Old maps are full of guesses. Where knowledge ran out, mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never seen and coastlines that bent the wrong way. Some added sea monsters, less from belief than from a need to decorate the unknown. As explorers returned with measurements, the guesses were slowly corrected, and the monsters swam off the page. But a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make. Every clean line was once a question, settled only by someone willing to sail past the edge of what was known and come back with an answer.

stimulus.title: The Unsent Letter
stimulus.text: Tomas wrote the letter three times before he stopped trying to send it. In the first version he was cheerful, listing the small triumphs of his new city as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown. In the second he was honest, and the page filled with everything he missed until it embarrassed him. The third version said almost nothing at all. He kept that one folded in a drawer. Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

stimulus.title: A Vault for Seeds
stimulus.text: Deep inside a frozen mountain, a vault holds something more valuable than gold: seeds. Hundreds of thousands of varieties of crops, gathered from around the world, rest in sealed packets at temperatures far below freezing. The cold slows the seeds' aging to a crawl, so that even after decades they can still sprout. The vault is a backup. If a war, flood, or disease wipes out a crop somewhere, a sample can be withdrawn and grown again. Its keepers hope it will rarely be needed, the way one hopes never to use a fire extinguisher. Its value lies precisely in being ready and almost never used.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Storms made the work dangerous, and isolation made it lonely, but ships depended on that faithful beam. In the twentieth century, automation arrived. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

stimulus.title: The Borrowed Violin
stimulus.text: Nadia had practiced on a school instrument so battered that two of its pegs slipped during every lesson. When her teacher handed her a loaner violin for the recital, she nearly refused; it felt wrong to play something so fine. But as she drew the bow across the strings, the tone opened like a window onto a bright street. Notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily, as if the instrument had been waiting for her. Afterward, returning it to its case, she understood that her old struggles had not been wasted. The fine violin had simply revealed the player she had quietly become.

stimulus.title: The Endless Material
stimulus.text: Glass has a quiet superpower: it can be melted down and remade again and again without losing quality. A bottle recycled today can become a bottle next month, then another after that, in a loop that, in principle, never wears out. Compared with this ideal, reality lags. Much glass still ends up in landfills because collection is uneven and because mixing colors lowers the value of the recycled material. Sorting by color and keeping glass out of general trash would let more of it re-enter the loop. The material is willing; it is our systems, the author suggests, that need redesigning.

stimulus.title: The Quiet Buffer
stimulus.text: Where the land meets the sea, a salt marsh can look like wasteland: flat, muddy, and crossed by winding channels. Yet this drab landscape does remarkable work. Its dense grasses slow incoming waves, blunting the force of storms before they reach homes inland. The same grasses trap sediment, letting the marsh build itself upward as the sea slowly rises. Beneath the mud, roots store carbon that might otherwise warm the air. For years, marshes were drained and filled without much thought. Only later did people recognize that the unglamorous marsh had been protecting them all along, asking nothing in return.

stimulus.title: Seeing With Sound
stimulus.text: A bat hunting in pitch darkness does not bump into things. It calls out, often at pitches too high for humans to hear, and listens for the echoes that bounce back. From the delay between call and echo, the bat judges how far away an object is; from subtle shifts in the returning sound, it can tell whether the object is moving toward it or away. A moth's fluttering wing returns a different echo than a still leaf. So precise is this sense that some bats can snatch an insect from the air in total darkness. The world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes.

stimulus.title: Dances in the Dark
stimulus.text: A foraging honeybee that finds a rich patch of flowers cannot simply tell the hive where to go. Instead, it dances. On the vertical comb, in darkness, the bee runs a straight line while waggling its body, then loops back to repeat the move. The angle of that straight run, measured against the pull of gravity, encodes the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the run signals distance. Watching bees crowd around and follow, researchers realized they were seeing a kind of symbolic language, one that passes precise information without sight, sound, or a single spoken word.

stimulus.title: Catching Water From Air
stimulus.text: In a few dry coastal regions, drinking water can be harvested from fog. Tall mesh nets are strung across hillsides where moist air rolls in from the sea. As the fog drifts through, droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and trickle down into troughs and storage tanks. A single large net can collect many liters on a good day, enough to supplement a village's supply. The method is not a cure-all: it works only where fog is frequent and winds are steady, and the nets need upkeep. Yet in the right place, it turns a passing cloud into a dependable resource, using little more than gravity and patience.

stimulus.title: Forests Beneath the Waves
stimulus.text: Off some cool, rocky coasts grow forests that no hiker will ever walk through. Giant kelp, anchored to the seafloor, can stretch dozens of meters toward the surface, swaying in the current like trees in wind. These kelp forests shelter fish, snails, and otters, much as a woodland shelters birds and deer. The kelp grows astonishingly fast, sometimes half a meter in a single day, drinking sunlight near the surface. But the forest is fragile. Where otters vanish, sea urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to bare rock, leaving a barren the divers call an urchin desert. A single missing animal can unmake a whole forest.

stimulus.title: The Coral That Keeps Time
stimulus.text: A coral skeleton grows in fine bands, much like the rings of a tree. In bright, warm months the coral lays down thick layers; in cooler, dimmer months the layers thin. By slicing a coral and counting these bands, researchers can read a record of past seasons stretching back centuries. Even better, the chemistry trapped in each band hints at the water's temperature when it formed. So a single old coral can serve as a kind of diary, written not in words but in stone, recording conditions long before anyone thought to measure them. The challenge is learning to read a language no one designed to be read.

stimulus.title: Travelers Without Legs
stimulus.text: A plant cannot walk, yet its seeds must somehow leave the shadow of the parent and find open ground. Evolution has answered this need with a surprising range of tricks. Some seeds grow papery wings and spin away on the wind like tiny helicopters. Others wear hooks that snag the fur of passing animals, hitching a ride for miles. Still others hide inside sweet fruit, counting on an animal to eat them and carry them off, depositing them far away. Each method is a kind of bargain struck with the world around the plant. The seed that travels farthest is often the one with the best chance to grow where the parent's shade cannot reach.

stimulus.title: The Secret Ballot
stimulus.text: It is easy to assume voting has always been private, but for a long time it was not. In many places people voted aloud or by a show of hands, in full view of employers, landlords, and neighbors. That openness invited pressure: a worker might think twice before voting against a boss who could see the choice. Reformers pushed for a printed ballot, marked alone and dropped in a box, so that no one need fear retaliation for an honest vote. The change seemed minor, a mere matter of paper, yet it shifted real power toward the ordinary voter, who could now decide without an audience.

stimulus.title: Stairs for Boats
stimulus.text: Rivers do not run level, and for centuries that simple fact blocked boats from traveling far inland. The lock changed things. A lock is a chamber with gates at each end; a boat enters, the gates close, and water is let in or drained out until the boat rises or falls to the next stretch of river. String several locks together, and a vessel can climb a hillside the way a person climbs a staircase. The engineering is humble, relying on nothing more exotic than gravity and patience, yet it knit distant towns into trading partners and turned shallow rivers into highways of commerce.

stimulus.title: The Stall That Listened
stimulus.text: Every Saturday, Mr. Owusu set out the same vegetables on the same table, and for years his stall was just one among many. What set him apart, his daughter noticed, was not his prices but his memory. He recalled which customer's child disliked onions, who was cooking for a crowd that weekend, who had been ill and needed something gentle. He would set aside a perfect tomato for one regular and toss an extra handful of beans to another. People did not return only for the produce; they returned because, at his stall, they were known. When he finally retired, the market felt larger and lonelier, though not a single other stall had closed.

stimulus.text: There was a time when a handful of black pepper could rival a handful of silver. The spice grew only in distant lands, and by the time it reached a European market it had passed through many hands, each adding a markup. Merchants guarded their routes jealously and spread tall tales about how spices were harvested, partly to discourage rivals. The high prices drove sailors to seek their own sea paths to the source, voyages that redrew the map of the world. In the end, the very abundance those voyages produced made spices ordinary, and the fortunes built on rarity quietly dissolved.

stimulus.title: First on the Rock
stimulus.text: When a bare rock is left exposed, the first life to arrive is often a lichen, a strange partnership of fungus and alga living as one. The fungus grips the stone and gathers moisture; the alga, sheltered inside, makes food from sunlight. Together they need no soil at all. As a lichen grows, it slowly releases acids that crack the rock surface, and its dead tissue mixes with grit to form the first thin crumbs of soil. Years later, mosses and small plants can take root in that beginning. The lichen will likely be crowded out by the very community it made possible, an unsung founder of the green world that follows.

stimulus.title: Letters of Lead
stimulus.text: Before the 1450s, a book in Europe was copied by hand, a task that could occupy a scribe for a year. Johannes Gutenberg changed that arithmetic. By casting individual letters in metal, he could arrange them into a page, print hundreds of copies, then rearrange the same letters for the next page. The cost of a book did not fall overnight, and many scholars still prized handwritten volumes. But within fifty years, presses across the continent had produced millions of books. Ideas that once crept from city to city now traveled in bulk, and a reader in one town could hold the exact words read by a stranger far away.

stimulus.text: It seems strange that people would farm in the shadow of a volcano, but many do, and for good reason. When a volcano erupts, it scatters ash rich in minerals such as potassium and phosphorus. Over years, this ash breaks down into some of the most fertile soil on Earth. Crops planted in it can grow unusually well, which is why slopes near certain volcanoes are crowded with farms and villages. The bargain is uneasy: the same mountain that feeds the fields can also threaten them. Farmers weigh the steady gift of rich soil against the rare but real danger overhead, and generation after generation, many choose to stay.

In this state it can endure boiling heat, the vacuum of space, and doses of radiation that would kill nearly any other animal. Years later, a single drop of water can revive it. Scientists are still untangling how the tardigrade protects its cells, but one clue is a special set of proteins that seem to harden into glass, cradling delicate structures until water returns.

stimulus.text: A white-crowned sparrow raised near San Francisco does not sing quite like one raised a hundred miles north. The basic melody is the same, but small flourishes differ from place to place, forming what biologists call song dialects. Young sparrows learn these dialects by listening to adult males during a brief window in their first months. A bird that hears no song in that window grows up to sing a thin, simplified tune. The dialects can drift over generations, much as human accents do, so a recording made decades ago may sound subtly foreign to the birds singing in the same meadow today.

stimulus.title: The Number That Was Nothing
stimulus.text: For much of history, there was no symbol for nothing. People counted sheep and coins easily enough, but the idea of writing down an empty amount seemed pointless, even unsettling. The breakthrough came when mathematicians treated zero not as the absence of a number but as a number in its own right, one that could be added, subtracted, and used to hold a place in larger figures. With zero, the difference between 5 and 50 could be written clearly, and long calculations grew far simpler. A concept that once felt like a riddle became the quiet hinge on which much of modern mathematics turns.

stimulus.title: Small Pieces, Wide Reach
stimulus.text: Plastic does not simply vanish. Exposed to sunlight and waves, a bottle or bag breaks into ever-smaller fragments until the pieces are too tiny to see. These microplastics have turned up in river water, in Arctic ice, and even in the bodies of fish and birds. Because the particles are so small, filtering them out of the ocean is nearly impossible. Researchers caution that the full effects on health are not yet clear, and they warn against easy conclusions. What is clear is that the cheapest fix is also the simplest: keeping plastic out of the environment in the first place, before it can shatter into pieces no net can catch.

stimulus.text: A great river carries more than water; it carries soil, scoured from distant hills and ground into fine particles. Where the river finally slows and meets the sea, it can no longer hold this load, and the sediment settles out, building flat new land called a delta. Over centuries a delta can grow seaward, fanning into a maze of channels and islands. But the process depends on a steady supply of mud. When dams upstream trap that sediment, the delta is starved; waves carry off more land than the river replaces, and the coastline begins to retreat. What looks like permanent ground is, in truth, a balance constantly being rebuilt.

stimulus.text: Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun overhead at noon. A traveler crossing the country adjusted a watch town by town, and no one minded a few minutes' difference. Railroads made the patchwork intolerable. So the railways carved the land into broad zones, each agreeing to share a single time. People grumbled at first about clocks that no longer matched the sun, but the convenience won out. The hour on the wall had become a public agreement rather than a private reading of the sky.

stimulus.text: The earliest ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. Built in 1817, it was a wooden frame on two wheels that a rider straddled and pushed along with the feet, like walking while seated. People mocked it, and rutted roads made it impractical, so it soon faded. Decades passed before inventors added pedals, then a chain, then air-filled tires that smoothed the ride. Each change drew new riders, and by the 1890s the bicycle had become a craze. It offered something rare for the time: cheap, independent travel that needed no horse and no rails. For many people, especially those long denied easy movement, the machine quietly widened the boundaries of daily life.

Experiment 1
Students placed a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water and set a lamp at distances giving several light intensities. They counted the oxygen bubbles released in one minute at each intensity, repeating each count three times.

stimulus.title: The Swaying Footbridge
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The bridge swayed from side to side on its opening day because of the people walking on it. When a crowd walks across a flexible bridge, small sideways movements make people adjust their steps to keep their balance. Many walkers end up stepping in time with the sway, and their combined footsteps push the bridge at exactly the frequency at which it naturally rocks. The more the bridge moves, the more people fall into step, so the motion grows. The sway appeared only when the crowd was large and stopped within minutes when the crowd was cleared, and no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The sway was caused by wind. As wind flows past the bridge deck and cables, it sheds swirling eddies alternately from each side, producing a push that switches direction at a regular rate. If that rate matches a natural frequency of the bridge, the structure rocks in resonance. The opening day was breezy, and the deck's flat shape is well suited to shedding eddies. Pedestrians certainly felt the motion and reacted to it, but their steps were a response to the sway, not its cause. Adding fins to the deck to break up the eddies, rather than limiting the crowd, is the correct fix.

stimulus.title: The Colors of Autumn
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The red and yellow colors of autumn leaves are simply revealed, not made. Throughout summer a leaf is packed with green chlorophyll, which hides yellow and orange pigments that are present all along and help capture light. As days shorten, the tree stops repairing chlorophyll and breaks it down to recover its nitrogen, and the green fades. The yellow pigments remain and finally show. Red colors come from the breakdown of sugars trapped in the leaf once the tree seals off the leaf stem. The display is a side effect of recycling, which is why a leaf's color has no clear benefit to the tree.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Red autumn leaves are produced on purpose. The red pigments, called anthocyanins, are not present in summer; the leaf makes them fresh in autumn, using energy and sugar at a time when the tree is shutting down. stimulus.title: The Perch of Miller Lake
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The decline of perch in Miller Lake began soon after the farms upstream expanded. Fertilizer washed into the lake by rain feeds algae, which bloom across the surface each summer. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Adult perch can move to shallower water, but their young cannot, so each year fewer fish reach adulthood. Reducing fertilizer runoff would allow the oxygen to recover and the perch population to rebuild.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2

Zander feed heavily on young perch, and their numbers have grown each year while the perch count has fallen. Low oxygen alone cannot explain the pattern: the lake had algae blooms for decades before perch began to decline, and nearby lakes with similar farms and blooms still have healthy perch populations but no zander. Stomach samples from zander in the lake contain mostly young perch. Removing zander by netting would allow the perch to recover even if the fertilizer runoff continued.

stimulus.title: The Swaying Footbridge
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The bridge swayed from side to side on its opening day because of the people walking on it. When a crowd walks across a flexible bridge, small sideways movements make people adjust their steps to keep their balance. Many walkers end up stepping in time with the sway, and their combined footsteps push the bridge at exactly the frequency at which it naturally rocks. The more the bridge moves, the more people fall into step, so the motion grows. The sway appeared only when the crowd was large and stopped within minutes when the crowd was cleared, and no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2

If that rate matches a natural frequency of the bridge, the structure rocks in resonance. The opening day was breezy, and the deck's flat shape is well suited to shedding eddies. stimulus.title: Why Songbirds Fly at Night
stimulus.text:

Most small songbirds migrate at night because darkness protects them from predators. Hawks and falcons hunt by sight during the day, and a small bird crossing open country in daylight is an easy target. At night the hunters are roosting. Night flight also lets birds use the daylight hours to feed and rebuild the fat they burn in flight. Birds that migrate in flocks during the day, such as swallows, are fast fliers that can feed on insects while moving, so they can afford the risk. The timing of migration therefore reflects a trade-off between safety from predators and the need to eat.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2

Night air is cooler and calmer, so a flying bird loses heat more easily and does not overheat during hours of hard flapping. Cool air also slows the loss of water from a bird's breath, which matters on long flights with nowhere to drink. The atmosphere is usually less turbulent after sunset, which lowers the energy cost of flight. Songbirds also navigate using the stars, a cue available only at night. Predators influence where birds stop to rest, but the decision to fly after dark is set by the demands of the flight itself.

stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The red and yellow colors of autumn leaves are simply revealed, not made. stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

stimulus.title: The Pebble Layer
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pebble layer exposed in the quarry wall was laid down by a fast-flowing river. The pebbles are well rounded, which happens when stones tumble against each other in moving water over long distances. They are sorted by size, with coarse pebbles at the bottom grading up to sand, exactly what a river deposits as its current slows. Many pebbles lie tilted in the same direction, the way a current stacks flat stones against the flow. The layer is also lens-shaped, thick in the middle and thinning to the sides, which matches the shape of a river channel cut into the older rock beneath it.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The layer was deposited by a glacier and the meltwater streams that flowed from it. Beneath the pebbles is a bed of unsorted material containing clay, sand, and boulders mixed together, a mixture that only ice can carry and drop in one place. Several of the larger stones have flat faces with parallel scratches, which form when stones are dragged along beneath moving ice. The pebbles above could have been rounded in meltwater streams at the glacier's edge, where sorting and tilting also occur over short distances. The region's climate records show it was cold enough for ice at the time, while river deposits need no such conditions.

stimulus.title: The Origin of the Moon
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision blasted molten rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it quickly gathered into the Moon. This explains why the Moon's rocks match Earth's in the ratios of oxygen isotopes, which differ from one body to another in the solar system. It also explains why the Moon has a very small iron core: the impact stripped mostly rocky material from the outside of the Earth, leaving Earth's iron core behind. The Moon's rocks are also unusually dry, as expected if they were once heated enough to drive off their water.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was captured by Earth's gravity as it passed nearby. Capture explains why the Moon is so large compared with Earth; the impact scenario should have left a much smaller moon or none at all, as computer models of similar collisions often show. The matching oxygen isotopes could result from the Moon forming in the same region of the solar system as Earth, from the same raw material. A capture would have left the Moon in a tilted orbit, and the Moon's orbit is indeed tilted relative to Earth's equator. The small core could simply reflect the Moon's original composition.

stimulus.title: The Vanishing Frogs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Frog populations in mountain streams across the region have crashed because of a fungus that infects amphibian skin. Frogs breathe and take in water partly through their skin, and the infection disrupts this exchange until the heart fails. The fungus has been found on dead frogs at every site where populations collapsed, and healthy populations remain only where the fungus is absent. Declines have spread from valley to valley in a wave, the way a contagious disease spreads, and have hit protected parks with clean water as hard as farmland. Frogs raised in captivity and exposed to the fungus die within weeks.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The declines are the result of pesticides carried by wind and rain from farms into the mountains. Pesticide residues have been measured in stream water, in frog tissue, and even in snow at high elevations. These chemicals weaken the frogs' immune systems, which is why a fungus that frogs have lived with for a long time now kills them. The fungus is found on many healthy frogs in regions with little agriculture, so its presence alone does not cause collapse. Declines are also most severe at sites downwind of major farming areas. Reducing pesticide drift would let the frogs resist the fungus as they once did.

stimulus.title: The Warm City
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The city center is about 4°C warmer at night than the surrounding farmland because of what the city is made of. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and store the heat, releasing it slowly after sunset. These surfaces are also dark, so they reflect less sunlight than fields and forests do. Vegetation cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, but the city has replaced most plants with pavement. The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights, when stored heat is released most effectively, and smallest in winter, when the sun is weak. stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.

stimulus.title: The Vanishing Frogs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Frog populations in mountain streams across the region have crashed because of a fungus that infects amphibian skin. Frogs breathe and take in water partly through their skin, and the infection disrupts this exchange until the heart fails. The fungus has been found on dead frogs at every site where populations collapsed, and healthy populations remain only where the fungus is absent. Declines have spread from valley to valley in a wave, the way a contagious disease spreads, and have hit protected parks with clean water as hard as farmland. Frogs raised in captivity and exposed to the fungus die within weeks.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The declines are the result of pesticides carried by wind and rain from farms into the mountains. Pesticide residues have been measured in stream water, in frog tissue, and even in snow at high elevations. These chemicals weaken the frogs' immune systems, which is why a fungus that frogs have lived with for a long time now kills them. The fungus is found on many healthy frogs in regions with little agriculture, so its presence alone does not cause collapse. Declines are also most severe at sites downwind of major farming areas. Reducing pesticide drift would let the frogs resist the fungus as they once did.

stimulus.title: Seed Soaking and Germination

Experiment 1
Students soaked batches of 50 radish seeds in water for a set number of hours, then placed each batch on damp paper towels in a covered tray and kept the trays at 15°C. After 5 days they counted the seeds that had sprouted and converted the count to a percent.

Results: at 4 h, 53%; at 8 h, 78%; at 12 h, 98%; at 16 h, 90%; at 20 h, 64%.
